intro: This unit is about two words that look alike and yet mean something quite different. Stopping (stilstaan) is only the immediate getting in or out of passengers and the immediate loading or unloading of goods. Every other form of voluntary standing still is called parking (parkeren). That difference decides everything that follows: which sign bans what, which places you have to leave clear, and where you may pull up for a moment but may not leave your car behind. Remember this side of it above all: a ban on stopping also bans parking, but a ban on parking does not ban stopping. At the end you also get the getting in and out itself and pulling away, because that is where every stop begins and ends.

body.tekst: Stopping (stilstaan) means standing still for the immediate getting in or out of passengers, or for the immediate loading or unloading of goods. The condition is that you are actually busy doing it and that it takes no longer than strictly necessary.

Parking (parkeren) is every other form of voluntary standing still. Leaving your car in a car park, popping into a shop for something, staying in your car to wait for a passenger, standing still to make a call on your mobile or to ask the way: that all counts as parking.
Two cars are standing still along the same road: someone is getting out at your car, while nobody is beside the grey car behind you.

A necessary stop in traffic is neither stopping nor parking. Pulling up for a red traffic light, pulling up to give way (voorrang verlenen) and standing still in a traffic jam therefore fall outside both.

The difference is not in how long you stand still, but in what you are doing. Letting someone out or carrying a box inside takes a short while and occupies the spot only briefly, so the law is relaxed about it. As soon as you start doing something else, or simply walk off, the spot is yours for an indefinite time and that is exactly what the parking rules are there to steer. That is why the exam looks at your intention first and at the clock only after that.

rijen: You let a passenger get in or out
You stay in the car to wait for someone
You pop into the shop for something
You stand still to make a call on your mobile
You are standing still at a red traffic light

body.tekst: There are places and situations where stopping or parking is not allowed, and signs can forbid it to you as well. Everywhere else you may stop or park, preferably in the places meant for it, such as parking strips (parkeerstrook) and parking places.

You may stop and park on the right of the carriageway (rijbaan) as well as on the left. The left has its drawbacks: you have to drive against the traffic and you have less view when you pull away again. On a one-way road the left can be easy and safe, because there are no oncoming drivers there.
On the left you may stay while you are busy, on the right it is called parking.

The word stilstaan sounds like any form of standing still, but in traffic it is a narrow term. If you are waiting in the car for someone who still has to come out, you are parking, even with the engine running and even if you drive off again after two minutes.
When letting people in or out you must not obstruct anyone either, and stopping must never last longer than the time you really spend on the getting in or out or on the loading or unloading.
Stopping is getting in and out or loading and unloading. Every other form of voluntary standing still is called parking.

body.vraag: You stay in your car to wait until your sister comes out. Are you stopping or parking?
body.uitleg: Waiting for a passenger does not fall under the immediate getting in or out, so it is another form of voluntary standing still and that is called parking.

body.vraag: You are standing still in a traffic jam. Are you parking then?
body.antwoord: No, and you are not stopping in the sense of the law either.
body.uitleg: A necessary stop in traffic does not count as stopping or parking, so a parking ban or a stopping ban does not touch you here.

U10-P02.titel: Bans by sign: E1 and E2

body.tekst: If sign [E1] stands beside the road, you may not park (parkeren) after it. Stopping (stilstaan) to load or unload, or to let a passenger get in or out, is allowed there.
If sign [E2] stands beside the road, you may not stop after it, and so you may not park either. Pulling up for a moment to let someone out or to load or unload is therefore not allowed there.
On the left the parking ban with its one diagonal stroke, on the right the stopping ban with the cross.
These signs apply only to the side of the road they stand on. If there is a sign [E1] on the right only, you may park on the left-hand side of the road.

Sub-plates (onderbord) can give extra information about the ban. If there is an arrow on it, the ban applies only in the direction of that arrow. If there are numbers on it, the ban applies only on those days of the month.

Signs banning parking or stopping do not apply to the parts of the road meant for parking, such as lay-bys (parkeerhaven) and parking bays (parkeervak). They apply only to the rest of the carriageway (rijbaan).
A sign [E2] stands along a street that has a parking strip. You may not stop on the carriageway there, but the sign does not apply to the parking strip, so in that strip you may simply park.

A parking bay is laid out for cars to be put in, so a sign that wants to keep the carriageway clear does not cover it. And because a sign always stands on one side of the road and points to that side, it can only forbid that side. Anyone who knows that never has to guess at such a sign: look at which side it stands on and where it points.

The book says that [E1] and [E2] apply to the verge as well, but it adds a footnote: after a court ruling that is no longer certain, and the CBR therefore asks no questions about it in the theory exam.
The two signs look alike and the difference is exactly one stroke. Always read the answer back: is the question about parking or about stopping, and which sign is standing there.
E1 has a stroke and bans parking. E2 has a cross and bans stopping, and with that parking too.

body.vraag: You pull up at sign [E1] to let your girlfriend get out. Is that allowed?
body.uitleg: The sign bans parking. Stopping to let someone get in or out stays allowed.

body.vraag: On the right there is a sign [E1], on the left there is nothing. May you park on the left of the road?
body.uitleg: The sign applies only to the side of the road it stands on, so on the other side nothing changes.

body.tekst: When stopping (stilstaan) you must not cause danger or obstruction. So do not stop before or after a blind bend or a blind hill, and not in places where you hold up the flow of traffic.

items: on a junction or a level crossing
on a cycle lane (fietsstrook) or on the carriageway (rijbaan) alongside a cycle lane
on a pedestrian crossing or within 5 metres of one
at a bus stop sign along the block marking (blokmarkering), or within 12 metres of the sign if there is no block marking
on a bus lane or on the carriageway alongside a bus lane
on parts of the road meant for other road users, such as a pavement or a cycle path (fietspad)

body.tekst: On the carriageway next to a cycle lane you may not stop, and on the lane itself of course not either.
At a bus stop you may let passengers get in or out for a moment, as long as you do not obstruct the bus.
On an advisory cycle lane (suggestiestrook) you may stop, but only if you cause no danger or obstruction. An advisory cycle lane is therefore something other than a cycle lane.

All the places on the list have something in common: someone else has to get past or across. A cyclist who has to go round your car ends up on the carriageway. Anyone standing still right in front of the stripes takes the view away from the pedestrian and from the driver coming along. So the bans are not there for the flow of traffic, but because your car makes someone else blind in that spot.
A stopping ban is the heavier of the two: where you may not stop, you may of course not park (parkeren) either. The other way round it does not work, because a parking ban simply allows stopping.
A stopping ban bans parking too. A parking ban does not ban stopping.

body.vraag: You pull your car up for a moment on the carriageway next to a cycle lane to let someone get out. Is that allowed?
body.uitleg: Stopping is banned on a cycle lane and on the carriageway alongside a cycle lane, so for the getting out as well.

body.vraag: At a bus stop sign without a block marking: within what distance may you not stop?
body.uitleg: If there is a block marking, the ban applies along that marking.

body.tekst: Where you may not stop (stilstaan), you may not park (parkeren) either. On top of that come the parking bans of their own.

items: less than 5 metres from a junction
in front of a driveway entrance or a driveway exit (uitrit)
outside the built-up area on the carriageway (rijbaan) of a priority road (voorrangsweg)
in any way other than the prescribed one, for example across a number of parking bays

body.tekst: In front of a driveway entrance or exit you may not park. Stopping for a moment to let someone get out is allowed here, because no stopping ban applies.

You may not park in parking places meant for another category of vehicle, such as taxis or lorries, and not in places meant for another purpose either, such as loading and unloading or charging an electric car. Places for particular drivers, such as disabled people or permit holders, are banned for you as well.
A disabled parking bay. Park here you may not, but letting someone get in or out is allowed.
In such a place you may stop, for instance to let a passenger get in or out or to load or unload.
Double parking is not allowed, not even next to a car standing in a parking strip or in a parking place beside the carriageway. Stopping to load or unload is allowed there.
Where you may not park, you may stop, unless a stopping ban applies as well.
Along the kerb there is a broken yellow line. Parking is not allowed there, but stopping for a moment to let a passenger get out is. If there is a solid yellow line, even that is not allowed.

A car that is parked stays there. That is precisely the problem at a driveway exit, at a junction and on a priority road outside the built-up area: the other person has to go a long way round it or look past it. Someone who is getting in or out for a moment is gone within half a minute and can still drive off in the meantime if that is needed. That is why the parking ban works out more strictly in such a place than what is said about stopping.
Two yellow lines along the side, two different rules. Broken is a parking ban, solid is a stopping ban. So read first which line is there and only then what you want to do.
Yellow broken: no parking. Yellow solid: not even stopping.

body.vraag: You leave your car in front of the driveway exit of a house to drop off a parcel across the road quickly. Is that allowed?
body.uitleg: You are leaving your car behind in front of a driveway exit and that is parking, and parking in front of a driveway entrance or exit is banned.

body.vraag: May you let someone get out in a disabled parking bay?
body.uitleg: Parking is not allowed there, but stopping to let a passenger get in or out is.

U10-P05.titel: Residential precincts, zones, the parking disc and paid parking

body.tekst: Inside a residential precinct (erf) you may only park on your own ground, for example under a carport, and in the places meant for it that are marked with a P.

The start and the end of a no-parking zone (parkeerverbodzone) are indicated with signs. Inside the zone you may not park anywhere, except on parts of the road meant for it, such as a parking bay, a lay-by or a car park.
In a no-parking zone the ban applies to both sides of the road, even if the zone sign stands on one side only. That differs from the signs [E1] and [E2], which apply only to the side they stand on.
In places meant for short-term parking you may only park with a parking disc (parkeerschijf). You recognise such a spot by the parking disc zone sign and by a blue stripe on the kerb.
The zone sign of the parking disc zone and the sign that marks the end of that zone.

The parking disc is compulsory for all motor vehicles on more than two wheels. You put it clearly visible behind the windscreen and you set it to the time of arrival, rounded up to the next full or half hour.

If you arrive at 12:40, you set the disc to 13, the next full hour. After that your car may not stay any longer than the maximum time on the sign, and setting the disc again in the meantime is not allowed.

items: Paying through an app: a sign beside the road gives the number of the parking zone, you enter that in the app, and when you leave you close the app
Pay-and-display machine: you get a ticket to put behind your windscreen, or you enter your registration number
Parking meter: you park for a certain time against payment, but topping it up is not allowed
Car park: you keep the ticket from the barrier, pay before you leave and put the proof of payment into the machine on the way out

body.tekst: A zone runs across a whole area and not along a single sign, so there is only one sign at the entrance and it has to cover everything inside that area. That is why it works on both sides of the road. With a parking disc the same idea works the other way round: the disc is the proof that you are standing there briefly, and it would be worth nothing if you were allowed to keep turning it on.
A zone sign on the right looks like an ordinary sign on the right, but it does something else: the zone takes both sides of the road. So look at whether the sign stands in a white zone frame.
A single sign: one side of the road. A zone sign: both sides, up to the end sign.

body.vraag: You park in a parking disc zone and arrive at 12:40. What do you set on the disc?
body.uitleg: You set the disc to the time of arrival and may round up to the next full or half hour.

body.vraag: The zone sign of a no-parking zone stands on the right only. May you park on the left?
body.uitleg: In a zone the ban applies to both sides of the road, even if the sign stands on one side only.

U10-P06.titel: Getting in and out and pulling away

body.tekst: Before getting in, look behind the car to see whether there is room to reverse if that should be needed, and then walk round the front of the car to the door. That way you see the traffic approaching properly and you see obstacles at the front.
You open the door only if that can be done without danger or obstruction, you get in briskly and close the door straight away, and then you put your seat belt on.

Before getting out, look in the interior mirror, in the left door mirror and to the left alongside the car. Get out briskly, close the door straight away and leave the carriageway (rijbaan) as quickly as possible, walking against the traffic.

If you want to pull away, you must let the rest of the traffic go first (voor laten gaan) and you must not cause danger or obstruction. Take account of your view and the room available, of the traffic approaching in front of you and behind you, and of the weather conditions.
You are ready to pull away, and a cyclist is coming up behind you over the very lane you want to move into.

kop: Order of looking before you pull away
rijen: On the right of the road
interior mirror and ahead, then the left door mirror, and last of all to the left alongside you
On the left of the road
interior mirror and ahead, then the right door mirror, and last of all to the right alongside you

body.tekst: If you are standing on the left of the road, bear in mind that the view is a good deal worse. Pulling away from the left-hand side is harder, because you have less view and because you have to cross over.

Before you pull away you must indicate, and you do that only just before you pull away. Indicate too early and other drivers may think your indicator has been left on, or they will be afraid that you have not seen them coming.
If you pull away from a lay-by outside the built-up area, be well aware that the other traffic is approaching fast. Make sure that after pulling away you also get up to the speed you want promptly.

Pulling away is the only manoeuvre in which you join the stream from a standstill, so everyone is faster than you and nobody expects you. You therefore need two things: a gap that is big enough and a signal that comes at the right moment. An indicator that has been on for a minute tells nobody anything any more.

Letting others go first when pulling away applies to all the rest of the traffic, so to the cyclist coming from behind and to the pedestrian on the pavement behind your car as well. It is not a question of who was there first.
Pulling away: look first, then indicate, and everyone goes before you.

body.vraag: You are parked on the right of the road and want to pull away. Where do you look last?
body.uitleg: First the interior mirror and ahead, then the left door mirror, and last of all to the left alongside you.

body.vraag: When do you indicate if you want to pull away?
body.antwoord: Only just before you pull away.
body.uitleg: Indicating too early confuses others, because they then think your indicator has been left on.
